paragraphs: A carrier strike fighter with canted twin fins, folding wingtips and the boxy intakes that tell the Super Hornet apart from the older Hornet. Fighter FA 18EF Super Hornet 2 spends 229,202 polygons and 234,434 vertices on that airframe. The budget keeps panel lines, landing gear struts and the tailhook crisp when the camera follows a low pass over the deck.

Surfaces carry 85 maps at 8192 x 8192 and 4096 x 4096, so stenciled warnings and gray paint hold up close. The UV layout is non-overlapping, and CheckMate Pro certification vouches for clean quads and tris with sensible naming throughout the hierarchy. Canopy glass and the dark radome sit as their own parts, which makes reshading them for dusk or carrier lighting quick.

Twelve versions sit together on this page, from the plain airframe at $179 to rigged builds for Maya and Cinema 4D at $219. There is also a configuration with weapons at $199, hanging stores under the wings for strike sequences. On sale since 2016, the jet has gone to 18 buyers working on flight sims, defense training and aviation film shots.

A small sprig of sweet basil with soft, cupped leaves, sized for garnishing a plate or a pizza in a food shot. Fresh Basil Leafs uses just 1,572 polygons and 1,583 vertices, so many copies can be scattered across a table without slowing the viewport. Each leaf has a gentle curl along the midrib, which breaks the silhouette and keeps the herb from looking pressed flat.

The 7 maps at 2048 x 2048 carry the veins, a slight gloss and the paler underside where a leaf turns toward the camera. Islands in the UV layout stay apart, and the StemCell standard means the same PBR look survives export to several renderers and engines. Translucency reads best with a backlight, so the leaves glow green rather than going dark against a bright window.

Published in 2020, this herb has been picked up by 18 buyers, mostly for recipe illustrations, menu renders and Italian kitchen scenes. It also works as a finishing touch on a caprese salad, a bowl of pasta or a cutting board beside a knife.

A ready set of orchard trees with fruit hanging among the leaves, meant for filling a garden, a farm plot or a backyard render. Buying the trees as one bundle saves the work of matching foliage density and bark style across separate purchases. Each tree stands on its own trunk with a rounded crown, so they can be spaced in rows or scattered loosely across a lawn.

The bundle carries CheckMate Pro certification, which covers clean geometry, real-world scale and consistent object naming across the set. That consistency matters when several trees share one scene and need to light and shade the same way. Colored fruit against green foliage gives a strong focal point in otherwise flat landscape shots.

Two sets are offered on the page: the original at $39 and Fruit Trees Collection 2 at $89, with a different selection of trees. Since 2020 the bundle has gone to 18 buyers, typically architects and game artists who need believable orchards quickly.

A saxophone in polished gold lacquer with every key cup, rod and pad guard modeled instead of painted onto the body. The Golden Saxophone spends 165,841 polygons and 172,063 vertices on that mechanism, which is where most of the weight goes. The flared bell and curved neck keep smooth profiles even when the lens sits right at the mouthpiece.

Its 22 maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 separate the bright lacquer from the leather pads and darker springs. No two UV islands share space, and the CheckMate Pro mark stands for tidy topology plus real scale for stage scenes. Strong reflections need an environment map, since a gold finish only looks rich when it has something to mirror.

The page holds six versions: golden, black and silver finishes at $79, and black, silver and plain alto saxophones at $59. Since it went on sale in 2016, 18 buyers have used the horn in jazz club interiors, music videos and band promo renders.

A garland of tropical flowers strung end to end, made to hang around a neck at a luau or a resort welcome. Hawaiian Lei puts 196,674 polygons and 228,037 vertices into the blossoms, so every petal keeps its own curl instead of melting into a tube. The loop falls in a soft oval, which lets it rest on shoulders or lie flat on a table.

All of it is quad geometry, so the flowers subdivide evenly when a camera pushes in for a portrait. Just 3 maps at 2048 x 2048 handle petal color and shading, keeping the file small despite the dense mesh. A CheckMate Pro rating and a UV layout free of overlaps mean no cleanup before the garland goes into a scene.

The garland has been sold since 2016 and has reached 18 buyers, often for beach resort ads, Polynesian festival scenes and character outfits. Draped over a dancer or a tourist figure, it instantly signals island holidays without any other prop.

A glossy yellow emoji ball with two red hearts for eyes and a wide open grin, ready for chat-themed graphics. Heart Eyes Emoji is built from only 1,218 polygons and 1,222 vertices, a light sphere that renders instantly even in animated loops. The hearts sit slightly raised on the face, so they cast small shadows and read as objects rather than decals.

Color, gloss and the darker mouth interior come from 5 maps at 1024 x 1024, more than enough for a social media frame. Its UV islands are kept apart, and CheckMate Pro certification guarantees clean naming and correct pivot placement. The pivot at the center lets the face spin, bounce or tilt toward the viewer with no extra setup.

At $9 it is an easy pick, and 18 buyers have taken it since 2020 for app promos, dating graphics and Valentine posts. Pair it with other faces from the same family to build a whole row of reactions above a phone screen.

Three steel beams welded crosswise at their centers, the classic hedgehog that stops tanks on beaches and city approaches. Hedgehog Anti Tank Obstacle needs only 12,573 polygons and 12,654 vertices, so a whole line of them can guard a coastline cheaply. Each beam keeps its angle profile, and the cut ends show where the steel was torched to length.

Rust and scale come from 5 maps at 12094 x 12094 and 4096 x 4096, an unusually high resolution for such a small prop. The unwrap has no overlapping islands, and StemCell certification keeps the corroded PBR look consistent across the formats delivered. Flaking orange patches near the welds sell the idea that the obstacle has stood in salt air for decades.

Two versions share the page, this rusty hedgehog and a Czech hedgehog variant, each priced at $19. On sale since 2020 with 18 sales behind it, the obstacle shows up in Normandy landing scenes, war games and modern checkpoint barricades. Placed half buried in sand, it reads as a beach defense; on asphalt it becomes a roadblock.

A ketchup bottle with a tapered neck, a ridged screw cap and a label wrapped around its body, ready for diner and kitchen scenes. Heinz Tomato Ketchup is modeled with 9,126 polygons and 4,582 vertices, a light mesh that still keeps the cap threads and shoulder curve smooth. The bottle stands steady on its base, so it can sit on a counter, a burger tray or a picnic table without adjustment.

The UV layout has no overlapping islands, which keeps the label artwork clean all the way around the bottle. CheckMate Pro certification confirms that scale is real-world, so the bottle sits correctly beside plates, fries and cutlery. A slightly darker tone near the neck suggests the thick sauce settling inside.

Released in 2022, the bottle has found 18 buyers, mostly for diner sets, editorial food stories and grocery shelf renders. Because it carries a real trademark, it comes under the Editorial Uses Only license. Placed next to a burger and fries, it is the quickest way to make a table read as American fast food.

An ice hockey helmet in team colors with a vented shell, adjustable side clips and a chin strap hanging below. Hockey Helmet Islanders spends 12,002 polygons and 12,172 vertices, enough for clean vent openings and a smooth rounded crown. The padding inside is visible through the open bottom, which matters when the helmet sits on a bench upside down.

Just 2 maps at 4096 x 4096 handle the shell paint, the team crest and the soft foam liner. The unwrapped islands never collide, and the build holds CheckMate Pro status, so it drops into a locker room scene at true scale. The glossy shell catches arena lighting in a long highlight that follows the curve from brow to neck.

Ten helmets are grouped on the page, including four plain red and blue shells at $49. The Islanders, Montreal Canadiens, visor and three generic designs each cost $39. Sold 18 times since 2016 to rink builders and game studios, it stays under an Editorial Uses Only license because of team logos.

A vulcanized rubber disc with a knurled rim and printed faces, the small black object every hockey shot follows across the ice. Hockey Puck 3 takes only 1,276 polygons and 1,278 vertices, all quads, so the rim grip pattern subdivides without artifacts. Its flat faces make it easy to slide along an ice plane in a motion sequence.

The 5 maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 carry rubber roughness, scuffs and the printed logo on the top face. Every UV shell has its own space, and the CheckMate Pro mark means real size, so the disc sits right next to sticks and skates. A matte black material with faint scratches keeps it from reading as plastic under strong arena lights.

Four versions are bundled on this page, from the plain Hockey Puck to official and classic ice hockey designs, all priced at $19. In the store since 2015, it has been bought 18 times for game props, slow-motion goal shots and sports promos.

A single hop flower with overlapping papery bracts, the cone brewers add for bitterness and aroma. Hop Cone is built from 3,157 polygons and 3,465 vertices, with each bract shaped as its own scale around the core. The cone tapers to a soft point and keeps a short stem, so it can hang from a bine or lie on a sack.

Color and translucency come from 10 maps at 2997 x 3523 and 2048 x 2048, giving the pale green tips a dry edge. Overlaps are absent from the unwrap, and CheckMate Pro certification adds clean naming plus true small scale. Backlit, the thin bracts glow, which is the look craft beer labels and brewery photos usually chase.

Since 2019 the cone has gathered 18 sales, mostly from people illustrating brewing guides, beer packaging and botanical charts. Scatter a handful beside a pint glass or a bag of malt and a brewery scene is half done. At $19 it is a cheap way to add botanical detail to food and drink shots.

An outdoor hot tub with molded seats, a wide rim and a water surface already filled to the brim. Hot Tub with Water uses 47,754 polygons and 52,125 vertices, split between the acrylic shell, the outer cabinet and the water. The seats step down at different depths, which keeps the interior from looking like a plain bowl.

The water is a separate surface, so it can be given its own refractive shader or swapped for an animated ripple. Its UV islands sit side by side without stacking, and the CheckMate Pro rating covers correct real-world size and tidy naming. Jets and headrests are set into the wall rather than floating, which reads well in a top-down shot.

First released in 2021, it has been chosen by 18 buyers for backyard renders, spa brochures and holiday rental visuals. Set it on a wooden deck with some steam and a towel, and the evening patio scene is nearly ready. At $49 it saves building a molded shell and water surface from scratch.

A full leg from hip to toes showing the arterial and venous network, with red arteries and blue veins branching down to the foot. Human Leg Cardiovascular System uses 13,458 polygons and 13,428 vertices in all-quad geometry, so the vessels stay round when subdivided. Main trunks like the femoral artery run down the thigh and split behind the knee into smaller branches.

Its 10 maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 separate oxygenated red from the darker blue of the returning veins. The UVs are laid flat without overlap, and CheckMate Lite certification marks the geometry as suitable for medical teaching. The red and blue coding follows textbook convention, which is what students expect on a lecture slide.

Two versions appear on the page: this circulatory leg at $39 and a muscular system leg at $49 for anatomy lessons that need both layers. Shown side by side, the two legs explain how blood supply follows the muscle groups. Since 2019 it has sold 18 times to medical illustrators, e-learning teams and vein clinic animations.

The liver with its large right lobe, smaller left lobe and the green gallbladder tucked underneath, shaped for anatomy lessons. Human Liver and Gallbladder is a very light build of 784 polygons and 788 vertices, made of quads that subdivide into smooth organ surfaces. The rounded upper surface sits under the diaphragm line, while the flatter underside shows where the gallbladder attaches.

Its look relies on 10 maps at 2048 x 2048, which give the reddish brown tissue a moist sheen and fine mottling. The unwrap is clean with separate islands, and the CheckMate Pro badge stands behind correct naming and real proportions. Because the mesh is so light, it can be animated or rotated on a web page without stutter.

In the catalog since 2019, the organ pair has reached 18 buyers among medical students, hepatology clinics and patient education videos. It suits diagrams of digestion, fatty liver explanations and surgery planning visuals where the gallbladder must be visible. At $39 it covers both organs in one light file for any anatomy deck.

A round virus particle covered in knobby capsid proteins, the icosahedral shell that makes papillomavirus recognizable under a microscope. Human Papilloma Virus HPV is modeled with 6,144 polygons and 6,146 vertices, all quads, so the surface bumps stay smooth and even. Its symmetrical structure looks clean in a close macro shot and still reads as a virus at small sizes.

The 5 maps at 4096 x 4096 tint the capsid and add a soft glow that suits dark scientific backgrounds. No islands overlap in the unwrap, and StemCell certification means the PBR materials behave the same in every delivered format. Duplicated and scattered with depth of field, a few particles turn into a convincing infection field.

Two versions are on the page, this HPV particle and a general virus and bacteria model, both priced at $19. Since 2019 it has sold to 18 buyers making vaccine explainers, medical lectures and health awareness videos. Cervical screening campaigns and dermatology slides are another common home for it.

A high-speed passenger train with a long aerodynamic nose, sleek white cars and a basic interior visible through the windows. Ice Train Simple Interior is heavy at 7,375,620 polygons and 3,807,968 vertices, most of it spent on bogies, pantographs and car joints. The interior is simplified, with seat rows that fill the windows without the cost of a fully furnished cabin.

UV shells lie apart from each other, and the train carries CheckMate Pro certification for real-world scale and clean naming. Cars are separate objects, so the consist can be shortened or lengthened to fit a station platform. A long continuous red stripe along the side helps the eye follow motion in a passing shot.

Released in 2022, it has found 18 buyers for railway animations, transport planning visuals and travel campaign shots. The dense mesh rewards close camera work, though distant shots may call for a proxy to keep render times reasonable. At $129 it is a full train set ready for a platform scene.

A tracked infantry fighting vehicle with a low hull, a turret pairing a large gun with an autocannon, and rear doors for troops. Infantry Fighting BMP-3 carries 701,956 polygons and 738,754 vertices, with much of that spent on road wheels, track links and turret optics. The wide hull sits low between the tracks, giving the vehicle its squat, boat-like profile.

Surfaces use 40 maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048, so hatches, bolts and dusty armor plates hold detail at close range. Overlap-free UVs and a CheckMate Pro rating point to clean geometry and real-world size for military simulations. Weathering gathers on the lower hull and fades toward cleaner paint on the turret roof.

Six versions share this page: green and desert schemes, static builds from $119 to $149, and three rigged ones at $179. The rigged builds suit scenes where the turret traverses or tracks need to roll. Since its 2017 release the vehicle has found 18 buyers, mainly for war games, defense briefings and documentary reconstructions.

A survival vest worn over a flight suit, loaded with pouches, buckles and harness straps that pilots fasten before a sortie. Jet Fighter Pilot Vest uses 24,584 polygons and 25,723 vertices, so seams, zipper teeth and webbing loops keep their shape up close. It holds a worn torso shape on its own, which makes it equally useful on a mannequin or a character.

The 8 maps at 4096 x 4096 bring out nylon weave, stitched edges and faded fabric. The texture space is unwrapped without overlaps, and CheckMate Pro certification fixes the size for fitting over a pilot model. Pouch flaps and D-rings are modeled separately, so small adjustments for fit do not tear the mesh.

Two versions are offered, this vest and a Military Jet Fighter Pilot Vest, both at $59. Since 2016, 18 orders have come from game studios, flight simulator makers and costume designers planning aviation films. Hung on a locker room hook, it also dresses a hangar or ready room scene.

A long-haul American semi tractor with a sloped hood, large chrome grille and a sleeper cab behind the driver's seat. Kenworth T680 Truck runs to 315,975 polygons and 349,388 vertices, spent on the grille bars, fuel tanks, fifth wheel and dual rear axles. The aerodynamic side fairings close the gap between the cab and the wheels.

The UV layout is tidy with every island in its own place, and StemCell certification keeps the PBR materials consistent across every delivered format. Mirrors, steps and grab handles are modeled as real parts, so a driver climbing in looks believable. Chrome on the grille and stacks needs a reflective environment to look its best.

Five versions are grouped here, starting with an exterior-only build at $99 and a semi truck at $119. This full truck costs $129, while two rigged options at $149 come ready for steering and wheel animation. Since 2021 the tractor has drawn 18 buyers for highway scenes, logistics visuals and trucking games, with the brand restricting it to editorial use.

A bundle of colorful kites in several classic shapes, ready to fly above a beach, a park or a hillside festival. The Kites Collection saves building each frame, sail and tail separately, which is fiddly work for objects that appear small in the sky. Different kite shapes give the sky variety when several fly at different heights.

CheckMate Pro certification covers the whole bundle, confirming clean geometry, correct real-world scale and tidy naming. Bright sail colors show well against blue sky, and thin strings or tails add motion lines in a still frame. Each kite is a separate object, so they can be animated swaying on their own.

On sale since 2015 and bought 18 times, the bundle has filled sky shots in children's book illustrations, holiday ads and seaside games. At $49 for the whole set, it is cheaper than modeling the kites by hand. Pair them with a few figures holding spools and a windy afternoon scene comes together fast.

A Russian electronic warfare system that mounts a large dish antenna on a multi-axle military truck chassis. Krasukha 4 1RL257 Mobile Electronic Warfare System totals 558,539 polygons and 605,018 vertices, built as subdivision geometry for smooth curves. The rounded dish dominates the silhouette and makes the vehicle instantly recognizable in a convoy shot.

Its unwrap keeps every island separate, and CheckMate Pro certification backs real-world scale and a clean object hierarchy. Equipment cabinets, ladders and the angular cab glass are modeled rather than implied, which holds up in close inspection. Military green paint across all surfaces lets it sit naturally among other army vehicles.

Four versions are on the page, with this static system at $149 and a rigged system at $179. The bare Kamaz 6350 8x8 Military Truck Chassis is also available, static at $129 or rigged at $159. Since 2020, 18 customers have bought it for defense analysis, war games and news graphics.

A compact six-axis industrial arm of the kind used for small part handling, machine tending and lab automation. Kuka Robot KR 10 R1100 is built from 69,346 polygons and 70,108 vertices, with motor housings, cable routing and the wrist flange all modeled. Each link pivots around a clear joint center, which makes posing the arm straightforward.

The 8 maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 cover painted housings, rubber cable sleeves and the metal tool flange. UV islands are spread without overlap, and the CheckMate Pro grade guarantees real size for placing the robot on a workcell table. A base plate with bolt holes lets it sit convincingly on a pedestal or a conveyor frame.

Eight versions are grouped here, including static builds at $59, rigged ones from $49 to $69 and Maya or Cinema 4D rigs at $99. White color variants sit beside the orange originals for cleanroom or lab scenes. Its 18 sales since 2015 come from factory visualization, robotics training and automation explainers, and the trademark keeps it editorial.

The large plastic tray travelers fill with laptops, shoes and coats before it rolls through an airport X-ray scanner. Large Grey Tote Tray Airport Security uses 5,582 polygons and 5,498 vertices, keeping the molded rim and rounded corners smooth. Its shallow walls and wide flat bottom mean props stack inside without poking through.

UVs are laid out without overlaps, so an airport logo or a printed advertisement can be applied to the floor of the tray. CheckMate Pro certification fixes real-world size, which keeps it aligned with conveyor rollers and scanner tunnels. The grey matte plastic shows faint scuffs well under the flat lighting of a security hall.

Three trays share this page: this grey tote, a tray with shaped boot recesses and a standard security check tray, each at $19. Since 2021 it has sold to 18 buyers building checkpoint scenes, travel safety videos and terminal walkthroughs. Lined up on rollers, a few trays are enough to show a busy screening lane.

A rounded lavender shrub crowded with thin silver-green stems and purple flower spikes, made for Provence gardens and borders. Lavender Bush spends 583,056 polygons and 940,852 vertices on the many separate stems, which is why the silhouette looks airy rather than solid. Each spike is made of tiny florets that cluster toward the tip, and the dense crown hides the pot rim nicely.

Just 3 maps at 1024 x 1024 handle color, which works because each spike is small on screen. The UV layout is mixed rather than fully non-overlapping, and the CheckMate Pro seal covers clean geometry and real scale. Placed in rows, a few bushes recreate the striped fields seen in summer travel photos.

Two versions share the page, this bush and a separate Lavender Plant, both priced at $39. Released in 2016, the shrub has reached 18 buyers, chiefly landscape designers, cosmetics packaging artists and garden centers. Its purple tone pairs well with stone paths, terracotta pots and white garden walls.

A US Navy littoral combat ship with a semi-planing steel hull, a broad flight deck aft and an angular superstructure shaped to reduce radar returns. LCS-1 USS Freedom Littoral Combat Lead Ship packs 583,525 polygons and 652,916 vertices into the hull, mast, deck gun and boat bays. A stern hangar and launch ramp let a helicopter and small boats work from the same ship.

Surfaces carry 25 maps at 8192 x 8192, so hull numbers, deck markings and weathered gray paint hold even in a tight shot. Clean overlap-free UVs and the CheckMate Pro label keep the vessel at correct scale in a harbor or on open sea. A low wake and spray along the bow will sell its speed in an action shot.

Six versions appear on this page, from a static ship at $269 to rigged builds for Maya at $249 and Cinema 4D at $289. On the market since 2016, the ship has found 18 buyers, mainly naval analysts, defense game studios and documentary teams.

An open leather planner lying flat, with stitched black covers, a ribbon bookmark and pages fanned across the spine. Organizer Open uses 23,198 polygons and 23,798 vertices, so the page curl and the rounded cover corners stay soft. Card slots inside the front cover give the desk shot a small, believable detail.

The 6 maps at 4096 x 4096 capture the grain of the leather, the thread along each edge and ruled lines on the paper. Islands in the texture layout stay separate, and the CheckMate Pro tag stands for clean geometry at desk scale. Soft shadows under the lifted pages keep the planner from looking glued to the table.

Two versions are offered: this black leather planner and an Open Weekly Organizer in red, both at $39. Bought 18 times since 2018, it shows up on office desks, productivity app banners and back-to-school scenes. Add a pen across the open spread and the scene reads as someone midway through planning their week.

A handful of classic interlocking toy bricks in bright primary colors, with round studs on top and hollow tubes underneath. Lego Bricks Set is built from 22,869 polygons and 22,899 vertices, which keeps every stud round and every edge slightly beveled. Bricks come in several lengths, so they can be stacked into small walls or scattered across a playroom floor.

A single map at 4096 x 4096 drives color for the whole set, which keeps material setup quick. UV islands are laid out apart, and the CheckMate Pro stamp signals real brick scale next to hands and furniture. The glossy plastic needs a soft highlight on each stud to read as the real toy.

First sold in 2016, the set has found 18 buyers working on toy store scenes, children's education videos and creative building tutorials. Because the trademark belongs to the toy maker, the bricks are offered for editorial use only. At $39 it fills a kid's room or a desk with instant playful clutter.

A second assortment of studded toy bricks, including plates and taller blocks that click together into small builds. Lego Bricks Set 2 3D Models comes in at 13,272 polygons and 13,292 vertices, made entirely of quads that subdivide cleanly. Rounded studs and the slight lip at each base make the pieces look genuinely interlocked when stacked.

One 4096 x 4096 map covers all the pieces, so changing a color scheme takes a single texture edit. Its UVs keep separate islands, and CheckMate Pro approval confirms the bricks match real toy dimensions. Scattered at an angle on a wooden floor, the pieces cast tiny contact shadows that sell the scale.

Since 2016 this set has sold to 18 customers for children's apps, play-based learning slides and craft blogs. Priced at $19, it pairs naturally with the first brick set for bigger, more varied piles. The toy brand keeps the model on an editorial-only license, so it suits stories, reviews and tutorials.

A wedge cut from a fresh lime, with juicy pulp segments, a pale pith band and a glossy green rind. Lime Quarter needs only 988 polygons and 986 vertices, which is light enough to sit on the rim of every glass at a bar. The cut faces meet at a crisp edge, so the wedge reads as freshly sliced rather than mushy.

Its 7 maps at 4096 x 4096 hold the tiny juice sacs, the dimpled peel and a wet sheen on the flesh. The UV layout avoids overlaps, and its CheckMate Pro rating covers tidy naming and true fruit scale. A light subsurface setting makes the pulp glow when a window sits behind it.

On sale since 2017, the wedge has been purchased 18 times for cocktail renders, Mexican food spreads and drink menus. Perch it on a bottle neck, a margarita glass or a plate of tacos to add a sharp spot of green. At $29 it gives drink and food shots a crisp, high-resolution garnish.

A set of cryogenic storage tanks for liquefied natural gas, with tall insulated shells, domed roofs and the pipework that feeds them. LNG Cryogenic Storage Tanks 3D Models Collection gathers several tanks in one purchase, so an export terminal can be laid out quickly. Access stairs spiral up the walls and ring walkways circle the roofs, giving the giant forms a sense of human scale.

The collection holds CheckMate Pro certification, which covers clean geometry, real-world scale and logical object names. Pale painted steel reflects sky color, so the tanks blend into coastal haze in wide aerial shots. Each tank is its own object, which allows rearranging the farm to match a real site plan.

Released in 2018, the bundle has reached 18 buyers, mostly energy companies, engineering firms and infrastructure documentaries. At $79 it fills a whole industrial skyline that would take days to model piece by piece. Pair the tanks with a moored gas carrier and a pier to stage a complete export scene.

A compact household stitching machine with an arched arm, a hand wheel on the side and a needle bar over the presser foot. Sewing Machine spends 20,431 polygons and 10,364 vertices on the body, dials and bobbin cover, keeping the curves of the casing smooth. The flat bed and free arm give a clear place to drape fabric for a working shot.

Overlaps are kept out of the unwrap, so decals for stitch patterns and speed markings can be painted cleanly. CheckMate Pro certification confirms household scale, which places the machine neatly on a craft table. Thread guides and the spool pin are modeled, which lets a spool of colored thread sit where it belongs.

This modern machine comes paired with a Mechanical Sewing Machine version, each priced at $39. Out since 2023, it has already found 18 buyers for tailoring blogs, craft course videos and hobby room interiors. Surround it with scissors, pins and folded cloth to stage a convincing sewing corner.

A pair of adult male hands with natural knuckles, creased palms and short trimmed nails, cut off at the wrists. Man Hands is ideal for first-person views, product demos and gesture close-ups where a full body would be wasted. Veins on the back of each hand and soft folds over the joints keep the skin from looking like plastic.

CheckMate Pro certification stands behind the build, confirming clean topology and correct adult proportions. The fingers rest slightly curved, a relaxed starting pose that is easy to adjust toward a grip or a point. Wrist openings are neatly closed, so the hands can attach to sleeves or float in an interface shot.

The page carries eight versions: two static pairs at $49 and six rigged pairs from $79 to $99 for Maya and Cinema 4D. The rigged builds save hours of weighting work when the fingers must type, hold a phone or wave. Eighteen sales since 2016 came from VR studios, medical illustrators and gadget animators.

A luxury Italian SUV with a long hood, a wide toothed grille and the three side vents Maserati puts on its front fenders. Maserati Levante 2017 Simple Interior uses 143,128 polygons and 162,381 vertices, putting the detail into the body, wheels and lights. Inside, seats and dashboard are blocked in simply, enough for tinted windows but not for a cabin close-up.

The 7 maps at 4096 x 4096 and 2048 x 2048 cover brake calipers, tire sidewalls and the badge on the grille. Thanks to non-overlapping UVs, paint changes stay simple, and the car is built true to scale under CheckMate Pro. Its deep paint responds well to a studio HDRI, with long reflections running along the shoulder line.

Three versions are on offer: this simple interior car at $99, a full Levante 2017 at $129 and a rigged one at $149. Since 2017, 18 buyers have placed it in street scenes, driving games and automotive journalism, as the marque limits it to editorial work.

A wide hand-stitched leather belt with an iron buckle and a tongue end, the kind worn by soldiers and townsfolk in the Middle Ages. Medieval Leather Belt holds only 1,134 polygons and 1,135 vertices, so it suits game characters as well as close renders. The strap follows a loose oval, ready to slip around a tunic waist or hang on a rack.

Its 4 maps at 4096 x 4096 show scratched leather, darkened edges and rust spots on the buckle. UVs are separate, and the CheckMate Pro grade signals clean topology plus correct scale for a human waist. Small punched holes along the strap tell the viewer how it fastens without needing extra geometry.

Since 2015 the belt has equipped 18 buyers' projects, from RPG characters to reenactment visuals and fantasy film costumes. At $19 it is an inexpensive finishing detail for knights, archers and tavern keepers. A pouch or a dagger sheath can hang from it to tell more about the wearer.

A black knitted beanie with vertical ribbing and a folded cuff, the plain winter hat that fits almost any outfit. Mens Hat Ribbed Beanie Black is a tiny mesh of 822 polygons and 824 vertices, all quads, ready to subdivide over a head. Its rounded crown sits snug rather than slouching, so it fits a character without cloth simulation.

The 3 maps at 4096 x 4096 render each knit rib and the soft fuzz of the yarn. There is no overlap in the unwrap, and CheckMate Pro approval confirms head-sized proportions. Black wool absorbs light, so a rim light helps separate the hat from dark hair.

Two versions are grouped together here: the ribbed black beanie and a Mens Winter Hat, each for $29. Since 2018 it has sold 18 times, mostly for winter apparel catalogs, street fashion renders and game characters. Folded on a shelf or worn by a skater, it signals cold weather instantly.

A steel ammo can with a hinged lid, a latch lever on the end and a folding carry handle on top. Metal Ammunition Case uses 7,772 polygons and 7,820 vertices, all quads, keeping the ribbed sides and lid seal crisp. The narrow rectangular box stacks well, so several can line a bunker wall or fill a truck bed.
